notes: Other villages are alive now, the way yours is. A village you know can split apart — and when it does, the breakaways may walk out of the treeline at dusk and ask for your fire, every one of them named. Your village votes on it at a moot, and the loudest voices on both sides say their piece first. Taking people in means more mouths to feed, and their reputation walks in with them: harbor the eaters and every other fire will remember. You’ll also hear about their hunger, their dead leaders, and their schisms through travelers — late, and not always right. And if a starving village comes begging — or comes with spears — that’s a real choice too.

When something with teeth is at your door, you can call for help four ways now: send a runner (slow, and the road is genuinely dangerous), light the signal fire (fast, but every fire for miles sees it — including the wrong ones), ask the System to carry the call (it's enthusiastic, it mistranslates, and it will collect a favor), or let out an ability cry like a War Cry (fast and honest, if your build earned one). Help arrives as a real party led by a named face from their village — and their foragers leaving their fields is a debt you'll repay, in food or in trust.

Once your village links with another, you can appoint someone to run the relay — the switchboard. Every message in and out passes through their hands, and they can hurry it, sit on it, or rewrite it. Choose carefully: your best talker costs the moots their voice, your weakest forager costs you the village's mood, and a schemer with the relay is a story waiting to happen. Watch the log.

Haven can grow now: stockpile food, wood, stone and preserved food and the village raises the Longhouse (room for 16), the Palisade (room for 20 — walls that bleed raiders and keep your sleep safe), and the Granary (room for 24, slower spoilage, a deeper famine reserve). The System tells you exactly what each one costs, the Haven panel shows your progress, and the village talks about what's missing.

The woods have teeth at night now: when monsters gather and the pantry smells rich, raiders hit Haven. Villagers fight them off for real — and anything they don't meet eats from your stores. There's a new stone-gathering job for the building pile.

Going national is no longer just lead-or-bow: you can confederate as equals — no throne, just a shared granary and a war-pact where every fire answers every call — or found a trade league that pays weekly tariffs but owes no swords. You can also take villages by force now: muster a war party, offer terms, or burn and subjugate — but blood has a price, and conquered fires can rise. And if the System offers you a polity, you can refuse the scale entirely: keep every kcal, answer to no one — and face the late waves alone.
Fan care packages are curios again, never dinner: the mislabeled BEANS can has stopped showing up in fan mail (the galaxy still thinks it is hilarious, it just stopped mailing it).

The wild got deeper: three new waves of monsters are out there now — the Final Draft, the Mirror Draft (built out of us), and the Producers themselves. They arrive when your deeds earn them, not on a schedule. One of them eats. It gets stronger every time it does.

The world got bigger: villages can now grow into something more. Lead a polity of allied villages — or swear yourself to one — and the System starts treating you like a power. Go far enough and the whole world starts watching.
The table got honest: humanity’s case is made of deeds now, not words. Waves fought, contests survived, standing earned, crises weathered — the invitation only comes when the case is real.

New on the title screen: Records. Every run feeds a permanent record of what you’ve encountered — plants, animals, monsters, milestones. New games still start fresh; the record is the reason to play again.

Fishing is honest now: your line catches real fish from the creek’s actual stock — creek chub and bluegill at their real size — and a fished-out creek tells you so instead of biting forever. Ponds hold smaller fish, like the water says.

The bear is a proper fight now. It mauls you every time you swing at close range — a spear's reach still halves it, but a knife up close is answered in full, every time. And if the bear puts you down, you stay down: no more walking away from 0 health.

Issue Challenge dares have real stakes now: if it comes to blows, the village holds you both to the terms — witnessed, to yield. Winner takes respect, loser takes humility. Break the terms with a killing and the village names you oathbreaker.
A delivered ratings stunt really moves the ratings now: when you give the galaxy its moment, the numbers tick up for real — and the System won't drag you back on camera off the same slump twice.
Watching the village's shows together pays what it promises: the good-snacks watch party brings the village closer exactly once, no hidden double-counting.

Issue Challenge is a real dare now: call someone out in front of everyone. The village hears it — the bold respect the nerve, some call it showing off. The bout comes when hands are thrown. Once a day.
End It Before It Starts actually ends it: your reputation walks in first and the dispute dies on the spot — but they will remember the look, and not fondly. Once a day.
Fighting abilities land the moment you use them: Brace is up before the counter-swing, and a War Cry can stop the hit that's already coming.

Haven's first link with another village is a moment now: the System's coordination layer comes online, and you choose Haven's first gesture — a gift of food, your speaker's three days, or cold ink. They're watching.
Village negotiations are played, not rolled: a village that won't take your terms counters with their own price — accept it, sweeten it with real food, or walk away from the table.
You can seal an understanding with a village, sealed with a feast — no tribute, no bowing. Their fire opens to your people: a guest's meal, once a day.
Diplomacy is knowledge-gated now: villages you've never heard of don't show up as proposals. Travelers' rumors actually reach you.
Corruption: a dark mirror to trust. What you do in the dark changes what you are — and people can feel it, even when they can't name it.
You can butcher the dead for meat now — and eat it. The first time will haunt you. It gets easier. That's the horror.
In a healthy village, discovered cannibalism means exile. In a starving or corrupted one, the rules change — and fear becomes its own currency.
Rare dark pasts: sometimes you wake as one of the village's hidden dark ones, with a history that explains it.
Running from a fight is no longer a coin flip — chasers chase you across the map now. Slow ones fall behind, fast ones gain on you, and you'll always see it happening.
The hushwolf does not give up. Once it's decided you're prey, only Haven's walls or killing it will end the hunt — the Codex says so, and so will the howls.
The wild things hit harder and take more killing than before. Armor is the answer: a geared fighter barely feels what flattens an unarmored one.
Fixed: your wielded weapon's damage bonus wasn't being applied at all — spears (and every other weapon) hit properly again.
Villagers fight with better judgment: they commit to fights they can win, call for help when outmatched, and only flee when it's truly hopeless.
The fallen keep their real belongings on the body — open the pack to take, leave, or use. Keepsakes are buried with their owner.
Crafting menu now shows every recipe you've seen, with honest odds. Villagers fetch their own armor and use the pharmacy before a healer.
The Craft screen now lists recipes you're learning — early attempts are honest blind tries (materials stay hidden until you've learned them).
Map monster popups no longer name creatures the village hasn't named yet.
Gristlefit rage can lash out at allies mid-fight — and now they remember it. Trust drops, and it haunts you.
Trying to strike an ally in a fight gets an honest refusal instead of silence.
